units.translation: To become overseers of the prayers that were made.
And that the good things be brought to fulfillment.
He endured to become the sacrificer of his daughter.
I do not think that death for this man will be ignoble.
To become far more chaste than her mother.
For the sake of good deeds I would have wished to become known.
He wishes to become liable to justice for his hands.
I remain to become a listener to this judgment.
They say that Io once became the keeper of the keys of Hera's house.
I do not know what I might become.
Become a wolf to the hostile army.
Many evils come to mortals from the land.
May there be trustworthy things for the land.
May such a one not dwell with me in the house.
May it be mine to sing in praise.
For to the prudent there are goads.
From which the dearest things come to mortals.
And I would have a long speech from the beginning.
So that he might become a deliverer for me from these things.
From where would I get a throne of the upper air?
If I could have a cloak like the sky.
For what relish could be better for a man than this?
May it be that when he comes, I may lift the dear hand of the lord of the house with this hand.
These allotted portions were fulfilled for us as we were born.
For we have been born from your blood.
And they were born because of evils.
Not to be born is better than to be born and suffer badly.
I may become, you may become, he may become, you may become
such things as he will suffer
this man will not be unburied
what shall I do? I become
I know (either by hearing or by experience), I understand.

[Attic form, for which the copyists generally substituted the common γινώσκω [I know], as has been said s.v. γίγνομαι [I become]. Aeschylus used forms of this verb besides the present: perfect ἔγνωκα [I have known], aorist ἔγνων [I knew], future γνώσομαι [I will know]. There is one example of the passive aorist, Suppl. 7 γνωσθεῖσαι [having been known].]
Second person of the future γνώσει [you will know] (in M constantly written γνώση [you will know])

with spondaic catalexis and a simple verb used for a compound, which the scholiast substituted, who explains: οὐκ ἐφ᾽ αἵματί τινι καταγνωσθεῖσαι ψήφῳ πόλεως δημοσίᾳ ἡμᾶς ἀπελαυνούση [not condemned for any blood by a public vote of the city driving us out], about which Lobeck spoke on Soph. Aj. p. 351 ed. sec., but without adducing any other examples besides this one.
Do you not know this, Prometheus, that words are healers of swelling anger?
One must bear the destined lot as easily as possible, knowing that the strength of necessity is irresistible.
I have known these things (τοῖσδε [these] is suspect, for which I have conjectured καὐτὸς [I myself]) and I have nothing to say in reply.
You will know that these things are true.
